units.title: Column- and row-parallel linear layers and communication cancellation
outcomes: Derive local outputs, weight gradients and input-gradient reductions for column- and row-parallel linear layers.
Implement a paired sharded MLP and reconstruct its forward and backward results against an unsharded oracle.
Explain why keeping the intermediate features sharded removes communication between the two projections.
units.why: TP changes which rank computes each part of one layer. A plausible forward output can hide a missing input-gradient reduction or a repeated bias.

next.note: Carry the paired projection layout into attention and SwiGLU.

study.title: Two matrix partitions and their composition
study.locator: Tensor Parallelism; Tensor parallelism in a transformer block, opening feedforward example
study.depth: Stop before the attention discussion. Do not gather column outputs when the next row-parallel layer consumes the same feature shards.

study.title: Megatron-LM: forward and backward communication
study.locator: arXiv:1909.08053v4, Section 3, equations 1 to 3, Figure 3a and Code 1

study.title: Weight storage and conjugate autograd operators
study.locator: `ColumnParallelLinear` and `RowParallelLinear`, including initialization and `forward`
study.depth: Also open https://github.com/huggingface/picotron/blob/59714b1bf25541dbeb6f5a721ed15f6d0768e786/picotron/tensor_parallel/tp_communications.py and read `CopyToModelParallelRegion`, `ReduceFromModelParallelRegion` and `GatherFromModelParallelRegion`. Defer the asynchronous operator.

focus: Use the paper's convention \(Y=XW\), then translate to PyTorch's stored \(W\) of shape \([D_{	ext{out}},D_{	ext{in}}]\). Column parallelism shards stored rows; row parallelism shards stored columns.

Column outputs own distinct features. Their input gradients are partial contributions that must be summed. Row outputs are full-shaped partial sums; their forward reduction must happen before adding a replicated bias.
An elementwise activation preserves feature ownership. Pair matching column output shards with row input shards instead of gathering and splitting again.
Megatron's identity-backward reduction assumes replicated outputs represent one logical loss, not separate independent losses on every TP rank. Reconstruct gradients under that contract.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive and simulate a bias-free column-GELU-row MLP on CPU with two shards, \(X\) shaped \([2,3,4]\), first stored weight \([8,4]\) and second \([4,8]\). Generate all tensors once with seed 0 in `torch.float64`, slice the same weights, and use squared-output mean loss. Match output, input gradient and both reconstructed weight gradients with `torch.testing.assert_close`. Then add one shared output bias after summation.
traps: Applying GELU to each row-parallel partial sum before reduction. Nonlinearity does not commute with summation.
Adding a full output bias on every rank before a sum. The result contains one bias per rank.
Comparing bitwise equality after changing GEMM partitioning. Floating-point reduction order changes; use a justified tolerance.

selfTest.q: Why does the first projection need a backward sum even though its forward pass is local?
selfTest.a: Each feature shard contributes to the same input. The full input gradient is the sum of those contributions.

selfTest.q: For stored weights shaped \([8,4]\) and \([4,8]\) on two ranks, what shapes stay local?
selfTest.a: The first weight is \([4,4]\), the intermediate is \([2,3,4]\), and the second weight is \([4,4]\). Each second-projection partial output is \([2,3,4]\) and must be summed.

selfTest.q: Does column-to-row pairing eliminate all communication?
selfTest.a: No. It eliminates the intermediate gather. With replicated block boundaries, the row output still needs a forward sum and the column input gradient a backward sum.

units.title: Vocabulary-parallel embeddings, output projection and cross-entropy
outcomes: Derive stable vocabulary-parallel cross-entropy and its local logit gradients without gathering full logits.
Implement vocabulary-range embedding ownership and preserve tied embedding/output weights.
Compare a CPU sharded loss with ordinary cross-entropy, then map it to PyTorch 2.14 loss parallelism.
units.why: Vocabulary logits can be much larger than the residual stream. Reducing per-token statistics avoids gathering them, but only if target ownership and the loss denominator remain correct.

next.note: Account separately for vocabulary logits and per-token reductions.
Test range boundaries, invalid targets and tied weights.

study.title: Sharded input and output embeddings
study.locator: arXiv:1909.08053v4, Section 3, paragraphs beginning 'The transformer language model has an output embedding' through the fused cross-entropy discussion

study.title: Vocabulary ranges and masked lookup
study.locator: `VocabParallelEmbedding`, especially `_vocab_range_from_global_vocab_size` and `forward`; `apply_tensor_parallel` final-projection replacement
study.depth: Use default dense lookup without padding or renormalization. Picotron gathers the final logits; use the loss-parallel route below to avoid that gather.

study.title: Loss-parallel layouts and current contract
study.locator: Apply Loss Parallel, Figure 2 and final-projection plan (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Open https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/distributed.tensor.parallel.html#torch.distributed.tensor.parallel.loss_parallel for the 2.14 contract. Keep the first implementation on a one-dimensional CPU mesh with class-index targets and no label smoothing.

focus: Build on Stable softmax, cross-entropy and loss reductions. For a token, reduce local maxima to \(m=\max_j z_j\), then sum local exponentials into \(s=\sum_j\exp(z_j-m)\). Reduce the target logit from its unique owner; loss is \(m+\log s-z_y\).
Each vocabulary shard computes its part of \(\operatorname{softmax}(z)-\operatorname{onehot}(y)\). Only the target owner subtracts one. Apply the same valid-token denominator as the unsharded loss.

Embedding ranks own disjoint vocabulary ranges. Nonowners contribute zero; summation reconstructs each lookup. Tied embeddings and output projections must share the same trainable shard, accumulating both gradient contributions once.

`loss_parallel()` requires class-sharded DTensor logits and backward inside the context. PyTorch 2.14 supports mean reduction only on a one-dimensional mesh; multi-dimensional token sharding needs sums or unreduced losses and an explicit global denominator.
units.reproduce: Without notes, split `torch.tensor([[1000., 1001., -1000., 999.], [2., -1., 0., 3.]], dtype=torch.float64)` into two class shards and use targets `[1, 3]`. Compute the max, exponential-sum and target-owner reductions, then the mean loss and analytic logit gradients. Match ordinary `torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy`. Repeat with class-sharded DTensors on two CPU processes using Gloo and `loss_parallel()`, comparing loss and reconstructed gradients.
traps: Normalizing each vocabulary shard separately. That produces multiple distributions rather than one distribution over the full vocabulary.
Treating every nonlocal token as an invalid global token. Validate the global ID first, then mask nonownership before lookup.
Padding the vocabulary and leaving padded logits in the softmax. Those classes change the denominator unless explicitly excluded.

selfTest.q: Why must the maximum be global before summing exponentials?
selfTest.a: All shard sums must use the same exponential scale. Independent local maxima require additional rescaling before their sums can be combined.

selfTest.q: Does averaging local vocabulary losses recover cross-entropy?
selfTest.a: No. Vocabulary shards partition classes for the same tokens. Combine their normalization statistics first; average only over the declared valid tokens.

selfTest.q: What gradient reaches a tied vocabulary shard?
selfTest.a: The sum of its input-embedding and output-projection contributions. Two independently updated copies are not weight tying.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: vocabulary-range lookup, stable sharded loss, tied-weight accumulation and loss/gradient comparisons in `trainlab`.
units.stopWhen: Your sharded loss and logit gradients match the ordinary oracle, lookup ownership passes at both ends of each range, and a tied-weight test accumulates both uses into one shard.

fit.note: Megatron v4 and Picotron cover embedding ownership; the tutorial's reduction diagram and 2.14 API cover loss parallelism, with the mini-project supplying tied-weight and gradient practice.

study.title: Aligned SwiGLU shards
study.locator: `swiglu`; `main` from gate/up/down distribution through reconstruction and gradient assertions

focus: Build on Multi-head attention: split, merge and gradients, MQA and GQA: sharing keys and values, and The modern decoder block. The new task is ownership and communication, not another attention implementation.

For whole-head sharding without KV replication, TP degree \(p\) divides both \(H_q\) and \(H_{\mathrm{kv}}\), and \(H_{\mathrm{kv}}\) divides \(H_q\). Preserve each query's KV mapping when slicing projection rows and output-projection columns.

When \(p>H_{\mathrm{kv}}\), a different plan may replicate KV heads among ranks. Their shared projection gradients must then be summed across the replica subgroup; the simple equally sharded plan is not legal.
SwiGLU gate and up projections use identical intermediate-feature boundaries. Their product remains sharded; the down projection produces partial residual-width outputs.
units.reproduce: Run the two named CPU examples below, then redraw their local projection and head shapes without notes. Extend a deterministic simulation to \(H_q=8\), \(H_{\mathrm{kv}}=2\), head width 4 and TP degree 2: each rank owns four contiguous query heads and their one KV head. With identical seed-0 `torch.float64` inputs and zero dropout, concatenated local attention must match the full GQA oracle. Reject degree 4 under the no-KV-replication policy.
traps: Splitting channels through the middle of a head and using the original softmax as if each shard had a complete query/key dot product.
Dividing query heads but forgetting KV-head constraints. Shapes may be divisible while query-to-KV ownership is wrong.
Pairing differently ordered gate and up shards. Their elementwise product then changes the MLP.

selfTest.q: Can eight query heads and two KV heads use four equally KV-sharded ranks?
selfTest.a: Not with complete KV heads and no replication. Two KV heads cannot give every rank one shard. A replicated-KV implementation is a separate plan with shared-gradient reduction.

selfTest.q: Why is an output-projection reduction still needed after local head attention?
selfTest.a: Each head subset contributes through a different set of output-projection input columns to the same residual-width output. Those partial contributions must be summed.

selfTest.q: Which intermediate dimension must both SwiGLU branches shard identically?
selfTest.a: The expanded feedforward feature dimension. Each gate value must multiply the up value for the same feature before the row-parallel down projection.

units.title: Sequence-parallel normalization and residual layouts
outcomes: Derive the all-gather/reduce-scatter boundaries between sequence-parallel norms and tensor-parallel projections in both passes.
Keep residual additions on matching token shards and sum replicated norm-parameter gradients.
Explain which saved activations shrink and which full-shaped temporary tensors remain.
units.why: Plain TP leaves the residual stream replicated. Sequence parallelism reduces its saved activation footprint while preserving full feature vectors for each local token.

next.note: Express these transitions as placement changes.
Separate saved-activation savings from temporary peaks.

study.title: Sequence-parallel normalization and residual contract
study.locator: Apply Sequence Parallel to LayerNorm/RMSNorm layers: block forward and adjusted parallelization plan (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Check `SequenceParallel` at https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/distributed.tensor.parallel.html#torch.distributed.tensor.parallel.SequenceParallel for sequence-axis defaults and the custom-initialization warning.

focus: For \([B,S,D]\) activations, each SP rank keeps \([B,S/p,D]\). Normalization reduces over features within each token, so it needs no cross-token statistics.

All-gather the normalized token shards before the column projection. Reduce-scatter the row projection's partial output along sequence before residual addition. Both operands then own the same tokens.

In backward, the forward all-gather has a reduce-scatter adjoint under this logical tensor contract; the forward reduce-scatter has an all-gather adjoint. Replicated norm weights receive different token contributions that must be summed.
The paper's activation formula counts saved tensors under its storage/recomputation choices. A transient replicated input does not disappear merely because the block's boundary layout is sharded.
units.reproduce: Return to TorchFeather's `tp_swiglu.py` from the previous unit. Without notes, trace `x`, `normalized`, `replicated`, `hidden`, `down_partial`, `down_sequence` and the residual output through both passes. With its two-rank settings, the residual shards are \([2,2,8]\), the gathered input and partial down output are \([2,4,8]\), and the intermediate feature shards are \([2,4,8]\). Confirm these layouts and the norm-gradient oracle on CPU.
traps: Normalizing across the sharded sequence axis instead of the complete feature axis. That changes the model and may leak future tokens.
Adding two equal-shaped local tensors that own different token ranges. Shape equality is not layout equality.
Leaving custom-initialized norm gains different across ranks. `SequenceParallel` assumes the usual unit initialization; synchronize custom gains explicitly.

selfTest.q: Why can SP normalization be local while feature-sharded normalization may not be?
selfTest.a: An SP shard contains every feature for its tokens. A feature shard lacks part of each token's normalization statistics.

selfTest.q: Why do norm weights need gradient reduction under SP but not necessarily under replicated plain TP?
selfTest.a: SP ranks process different tokens, so each gradient is a contribution to the shared weight. Plain TP replicated norms can compute identical complete gradients under identical input and loss semantics.

selfTest.q: Does replacing an all-reduce with an all-gather plus reduce-scatter guarantee equal step time?
selfTest.a: No. Ideal ring payloads can match, but launch count, ordering, buffers, kernel shapes and extra re-gathers can differ.
